question: What are the common symptoms of diabetes?
expected_answer: Common symptoms of diabetes include frequent urination (especially at night), excessive thirst, unexplained weight loss, increased hunger, fatigue, blurred vision, slow-healing cuts, frequent infections, tingling/numbness in hands and feet, and dry itchy skin. Some people with Type 2 diabetes may have no symptoms initially.
reference_context: Diabetes Mellitus Patient Education Guide: Classic symptoms of high blood sugar (hyperglycemia) include: Frequent urination (polyuria) - especially at night; Excessive thirst (polydipsia); Unexplained weight loss; Increased hunger (polyphagia); Fatigue and weakness; Blurred vision; Slow-healing cuts and bruises; Frequent infections; Tingling or numbness in hands and feet (neuropathy); Dry, itchy skin. Note: Some people with Type 2 diabetes may have no symptoms initially.

question: How is Type 2 diabetes managed?
expected_answer: Type 2 diabetes management includes lifestyle modifications (healthy eating with controlled carbohydrates, regular physical activity 150+ minutes/week, weight management, blood glucose monitoring, smoking cessation, limited alcohol) and medications (Metformin as first-line, Sulfonylureas, DPP-4 inhibitors, SGLT2 inhibitors, GLP-1 receptor agonists, insulin when oral medications are insufficient).
reference_context: Diabetes Mellitus Patient Education Guide: Management and Treatment - Lifestyle Modifications (Cornerstone for Type 2): Healthy eating: balanced diet with controlled carbohydrates, high fiber, lean proteins; Regular physical activity: at least 150 minutes/week of moderate exercise; Weight management: 5-10% weight loss can significantly improve blood sugar control; Blood glucose monitoring; Smoking cessation; Limited alcohol consumption. Medications for Type 2 Diabetes: Metformin: First-line therapy, improves insulin sensitivity; Sulfonylureas (glipizide, glimepiride): Stimulate insulin release; DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, linagliptin): Increase incretin levels; SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin, dapagliflozin): Reduce glucose reabsorption in kidneys; GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide): Enhance insulin secretion, slow gastric emptying; Insulin therapy: When oral medications are insufficient.

question: When should I consult a doctor for diabetes?
expected_answer: Consult a doctor if you experience diabetes symptoms, have risk factors and haven't been screened, have consistently high blood sugar, experience hypoglycemia symptoms (shaking, sweating, confusion, rapid heartbeat), develop signs of infection or slow-healing wounds/foot problems, or before starting new exercise/diet programs. Regular check-ups every 3-6 months are recommended for monitoring.
reference_context: Diabetes Mellitus Patient Education Guide: When to Consult a Doctor: If you experience any symptoms of diabetes; If you have risk factors and haven't been screened; If diagnosed with diabetes and blood sugar is consistently above target; If you experience symptoms of hypoglycemia (shaking, sweating, confusion, rapid heartbeat); If you develop signs of infection, slow-healing wounds, or foot problems; Before starting new exercise programs or making major diet changes; Regular check-ups every 3-6 months for monitoring HbA1c, kidney function, eye exams, foot exams.

question: What is the difference between Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes?
expected_answer: Type 1 diabetes is an autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks insulin-producing beta cells, usually diagnosed in children/teens/young adults, requires lifelong insulin therapy (5-10% of cases). Type 2 diabetes is the most common form (90-95% of cases) where the body becomes resistant to insulin or doesn't produce enough, often associated with overweight/inactivity/family history, usually diagnosed in adults but increasingly in younger people, can often be managed with lifestyle changes and oral medications.
reference_context: Diabetes Mellitus Patient Education Guide: Type 1 Diabetes - An autoimmune condition where the immune system attacks insulin-producing beta cells in the pancreas; Usually diagnosed in children, teens, and young adults; Requires lifelong insulin therapy; Accounts for approximately 5-10% of diabetes cases. Type 2 Diabetes - The most common form, accounting for 90-95% of diabetes cases; Develops when the body becomes resistant to insulin or doesn't produce enough insulin; Often associated with overweight, physical inactivity, and family history; Usually diagnosed in adults, but increasingly seen in younger people; Can often be managed with lifestyle changes, oral medications, and sometimes insulin.

question: What are the risk factors for Type 2 diabetes?
expected_answer: Risk factors for Type 2 diabetes include: overweight/obesity (BMI ≥ 25), physical inactivity, family history of diabetes, age 45 or older, high blood pressure (≥ 140/90 mmHg), abnormal cholesterol (low HDL, high triglycerides), history of gestational diabetes, PCOS, and certain ethnic backgrounds (African American, Hispanic, Native American, Asian American).
reference_context: Diabetes Mellitus Patient Education Guide: Risk Factors for Type 2 Diabetes - Overweight or obesity (BMI ≥ 25); Physical inactivity; Family history of diabetes; Age 45 or older; High blood pressure (≥ 140/90 mmHg); Abnormal cholesterol levels (low HDL, high triglycerides); History of gestational diabetes; Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS); Certain ethnic backgrounds (African American, Hispanic, Native American, Asian American).

question: What are the complications of uncontrolled diabetes?
expected_answer: Uncontrolled diabetes can lead to short-term complications: diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA - life-threatening, more common in Type 1), hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS - life-threatening, more common in Type 2), and hypoglycemia from medications. Long-term complications include: cardiovascular disease (heart attack, stroke), kidney damage (nephropathy), nerve damage (neuropathy), eye damage (retinopathy), foot problems (potentially leading to amputation), and skin conditions/infections.
reference_context: Diabetes Mellitus Patient Education Guide: Complications of Uncontrolled Diabetes - Short-term: Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) - life-threatening, more common in Type 1; Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state (HHS) - life-threatening, more common in Type 2; Hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) from medications. Long-term: Cardiovascular disease (heart attack, stroke); Kidney damage (nephropathy) leading to kidney failure; Nerve damage (neuropathy) causing pain, numbness, digestive issues; Eye damage (retinopathy) leading to blindness; Foot problems potentially leading to amputation; Skin conditions and infections.

question: How can I prevent Type 2 diabetes?
expected_answer: Prevention of Type 2 diabetes includes: maintaining a healthy weight, eating a balanced diet rich in whole grains/fruits/vegetables/lean proteins, engaging in regular physical activity, avoiding prolonged sedentary behavior, and getting regular health screenings if at risk.
reference_context: Diabetes Mellitus Patient Education Guide: Prevention of Type 2 Diabetes - Maintain a healthy weight; Eat a balanced diet rich in whole grains, fruits, vegetables, lean proteins; Engage in regular physical activity; Avoid prolonged sedentary behavior; Get regular health screenings if at risk.

question: What is gestational diabetes?
expected_answer: Gestational diabetes develops during pregnancy and usually resolves after delivery. However, it increases the risk of developing Type 2 diabetes later in life.
reference_context: Diabetes Mellitus Patient Education Guide: Gestational Diabetes - Develops during pregnancy; Usually resolves after delivery; Increases risk of developing Type 2 diabetes later in life.

question: How is diabetes diagnosed?
expected_answer: Diabetes is diagnosed through blood tests: fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L), HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (48 mmol/mol), random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) with symptoms, or oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) 2-hour glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL.
reference_context: Diabetes Mellitus Patient Education Guide: Diagnosis - Diabetes is diagnosed through blood tests: Fasting plasma glucose ≥ 126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L); HbA1c ≥ 6.5% (48 mmol/mol); Random plasma glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L) with symptoms; Oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT) 2-hour glucose ≥ 200 mg/dL.
